questions.text:
Consider the language L over the alphabet {0, 1}, given below:

[latex]L = \{w \in \{0, 1\}^* | w \text{ does not contain three or more consecutive 1's} \}.[/latex]
The minimum number of states in a Deterministic Finite-State Automaton (DFA) for L is _____.
questions.solution:
The DFA only needs to remember how many 1s have just been seen in a row:
- q0: last symbol 0 (or start)
- q1: one 1
- q2: two 1s
- q3: three 1s seen [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] dead (non-final) state

q0, q1, q2 are final. A 0 returns q0/q1/q2 to q0. All 4 states are distinguishable.

Answer: 4

questions.text:
Consider the pushdown automaton (PDA) [latex]P[/latex] below, which runs on the input alphabet [latex]\{a,b\}[/latex], has stack alphabet [latex] \{ \perp ,A\}[/latex], and has three states [latex] \{s,p,q\}[/latex], with [latex]s[/latex] being the start state. A transition from state [latex]u[/latex] to state [latex]v[/latex] , labelled [latex]c/X/\gamma [/latex] , where [latex]c[/latex] is an input symbol or , [latex]X[/latex] is a stack symbol, and [latex]\gamma [/latex] is a string of stack symbols, represents the fact that in state [latex]u[/latex], the PDA can read [latex]c[/latex] from the input, with [latex]X[/latex] on the top of its stack, pop [latex]X[/latex] from the stack, push in the string [latex]\gamma [/latex] on the stack, and go to state [latex]v[/latex]. In the initial configuration, the stack has only the symbol [latex]\perp [/latex] in it. The PDA accepts by empty stack.

Which one of the following options correctly describes the language accepted by [latex]P[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Read the PDA transitions:
- In s, every a pushes an A (so m a's give m A's).
- The first b moves to p and pops an A; each further b pops another A.
- To empty the stack we must go to q, and both moves into q need an A on top. In q, the remaining A's and [latex]\perp[/latex] are popped.

So at least one A must be left after reading the b's: [latex]n \lt m[/latex], and [latex]m\ge1[/latex] (with no a's there is no A to move to q).

Answer: [latex]\{a^mb^n\mid 1\le m,\ n \lt m\}[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.text:
Consider the context-free grammar [latex]G[/latex] below
[latex] S\rightarrow aSb \;| \;X[/latex]
[latex] X\rightarrow aX \;| \;Xb \;|\; a\;|\; b[/latex]
where [latex]S[/latex] and [latex]X[/latex] are non-terminals, and [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are terminal symbols. The starting non-terminal is [latex]S[/latex].
Which one of the following statements is CORRECT?
questions.solution:
X: [latex]X\rightarrow aX[/latex] adds a's on the left, [latex]X\rightarrow Xb[/latex] adds b's on the right, ending with a or b. So [latex]L(X)=a^*(a+b)b^*[/latex].

[latex]S\rightarrow aSb[/latex] only adds more a's on the left and more b's on the right of X, so the result stays in [latex]a^*(a+b)b^*[/latex] and covers all of it (use S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] X directly).

This is regular, and it is not [latex](a+b)^*[/latex] (e.g. "ba" is missing).

Answer: The language generated by G is [latex]a^*(a+b)b^*[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The language generated by [latex] G \text{ is }(a + b)^*[/latex]
The language generated by [latex] G \text{ is } a^*(a + b)b^*[/latex]
The language generated by [latex] G \text{ is }a^*b^*(a + b)[/latex]
The language generated by [latex] G[/latex] is not a regular language

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Regular languages are closed under intersection [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- CFLs are not closed under intersection: [latex]a^nb^nc^m\cap a^mb^nc^n=a^nb^nc^n[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Recursive: run both deciders, accept if both accept [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- RE: run both recognizers, accept when both accept [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 1, 3 and 4

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The intersection of two regular languages is regular.
The intersection of two context-free languages is context-free.
The intersection of two recursive languages is recursive.
The intersection of two recursively enumerable languages is recursively enumerable.

questions.text:
Consider the following definition of a lexical token [latex]id[/latex] for an identifier in a programming language, using extended regular expressions:

[latex] letter \rightarrow [A-Za-z][/latex]
[latex] digit \rightarrow [0-9][/latex]
[latex] id \rightarrow letter (letter\;| \;digit)^*[/latex]


Which one of the following Non-deterministic Finite-state Automata with - transitions accepts the set of valid identifiers? (A double-circle denotes a final state)
questions.solution:
An identifier is one letter followed by any mix of letters and digits.

- (A): the [latex]\epsilon[/latex] edge lets the string skip the first letter, e.g. "1" or the empty string is accepted [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.
- (B): after choosing a branch you stay with only letters or only digits; "a1b" is rejected [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.
- (C): letter, then from the final state any number of letter-or-digit steps through the loop [latex]\text{---}[/latex] correct.
- (D): forces "letter digit" pairs; "ab" is rejected [latex]\text{---}[/latex] wrong.

Answer: C
